# Mutants charter-core does not catch yet — the backlog the nightly measures against.
#
# `.github/workflows/mutants.yml`'s `survivors` job is red when it finds a survivor that is
# NOT in this file. Without that, it would be red every single night and mean nothing: the
# run of 2026-09-21 found 141 survivors in the 38% of the crate it managed to test before
# GitHub killed it, and the whole crate is likely to hold two or three times that.
#
# So this file is the difference between "charter-core has a coverage backlog", which is a
# fact about today, and "something got worse last night", which is news. Only the second one
# turns the nightly red.
#
# **It is a backlog and not an absolution.** Every line is a change to charter-core that no
# test notices, including fourteen in `leakguard.rs`, which is the guard that stops a
# credential reaching a model. Deleting a line by writing the test is the point of the file.
#
# Three rules:
#
#   * A line is `<file>: <the mutation, as cargo-mutants describes it>` — deliberately NOT
#     `file:line:col`, so that editing above a mutant does not make it look new.
#   * Adding a line is a decision with a reason, made in the PR that adds it. A mutation that
#     genuinely cannot change any answer does not belong here at all: prove it, and say so in
#     the source where the next reader will be standing. `realpath` in `pypath.rs` carries the
#     worked example — and the lesson that its three "inert" mutations were catchable once a
#     redundant guard stopped absorbing them.
#   * Removing a line is free and never red. The `survivors` job lists the ones a test has
#     started catching so they can be pruned.
#
# Seeded from run 35580456628 (2026-09-21), shards 0, 1 and 3 — 38% coverage, so the first
# run that finishes the whole crate WILL report a large batch of genuinely untested mutants.
# That run's summary attaches the full set as `mutants-survivors.current.txt`; re-seeding from
# it is a copy, and it is a decision to make deliberately rather than a chore to automate.
